summary: Identifies the need for DNS extensions to Network Address Translators and outlines how a DNS Application Level Gateway can meet it. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2694 explains how a helper in a Network Address Translator can change addresses inside DNS messages. This lets a DNS name point to an address that works in the network asking the question.

questions: how does dns work with nat
why do dns addresses change with nat
how does dns alg work with nat
subtitle: How DNS answers can reflect address translation between private and external networks.

tldr.problem: A Network Address Translator changes packet addresses, but DNS records can also contain addresses. A private address in a DNS answer may not work for a host on the other side of the translator.
tldr.mechanism: A DNS Application Level Gateway works with NAT state to replace addresses inside DNS questions and answers as packets cross address realms. Dynamic bindings can be held temporarily after a lookup and committed when a session begins.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes the need, behavior and limits of DNS_ALG for several NAT arrangements. It is Informational and does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2694 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DNS and NAT Can Disagree
sections.content:
A Network Address Translator (NAT) changes IP addresses in packet headers as traffic moves between address realms. Applications may also put an IP address inside their data, which NAT normally does not change.

DNS maps host names to addresses. A DNS answer containing a private address may be unusable outside that private realm. RFC 2694 describes a DNS Application Level Gateway (DNS_ALG) that edits DNS payloads using address-binding information held by NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT changes addresses on the outside of a packet. DNS_ALG can also change an address written inside a DNS message, so the answer fits the network that asked.

sections.title: Temporary and Committed Bindings
sections.content:
A static binding always maps a private address to the same external address. A dynamic binding can change. For dynamic addresses, DNS_ALG may ask NAT for a temporary binding when a DNS answer is prepared; the binding becomes committed when a session starts using it.

A configurable Bind-holdout time limits how long an unused temporary binding remains active. The memo notes that NAT may limit such bindings to reduce denial-of-service attempts that request names without starting sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS lookup can reserve an outside address for a short time. If a connection uses it, NAT keeps the mapping for that session; otherwise it can release the reservation.

sections.title: Changing DNS Questions and Answers
sections.content:
For an incoming name-to-address lookup, DNS_ALG leaves the question unchanged. When the private DNS server returns an address, the gateway replaces it with the assigned external address. For reverse lookups, it can translate the address in the query and in the reply when a binding exists; otherwise it may refuse the query.

Dynamic address answers receive a Time To Live of zero so they are not cached; the memo notes that a value of one may work better with broken implementations. DNS_ALG also has to update checksums and, when payload length changes, TCP sequence information and compressed-name offsets.
sections.plainLanguage: For an outside lookup, DNS_ALG can replace the private address in the answer with the address NAT assigned outside. Dynamic answers should not be kept in a cache after the lookup.

sections.title: Limits and Security
sections.content:
DNS_ALG cannot edit a DNS message protected by DNSSEC without invalidating its protection. The memo says secure DNS replies crossing address realms will therefore fail, unless the gateway has the keys needed to verify and modify the data.

Dynamic bindings also create a denial-of-service risk if an attacker repeatedly causes unused temporary mappings to be allocated. The memo suggests limiting temporary bindings or rejecting requests that would exceed such limits.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway cannot safely rewrite a DNS answer that has a digital signature unless it can verify and protect the changed answer. Repeated lookups can also consume temporary address mappings.
